\section*{Score Advanced papers}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA01-P2-PHY-S3-Q03, source={Score Advanced - Test 01 (22 Sep 2020)}, paper=2, qno=3, type=numerical, subtopic={Expansion}, answer={2.50}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: glass bulb weighed in liquid, expansion | steps: apparent weights; expansion of glass; liquid coefficient}]
A glass bulb with volumetric expansion coefficient $\alpha=1.50\times10^{-5}\ {}^0\mathrm C^{-1}$ is weighed in liquid at temperatures t = 10$^0$C and t$_1$ = 20$^0$C. The weights of the displaced liquids are p = 100.01 g and p$_1$ = 100 g respectively. Find the volumetric expansion coefficient $\alpha_1$ (in the units of $10^{-5}\ {}^0\mathrm C^{-1}$) of the liquid in the temperature interval from t to t$_1$.
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA08-P2-PHY-S3-Q03, source={Score Advanced - Test 08 (22 Apr 2023)}, paper=2, qno=3, type=numerical, subtopic={Specific and latent heat}, answer={6}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K3 S1 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: heating power to boil water continuously, specific and latent heat, heat to raise 40 C to 100 C plus the heat to vaporise the water | steps: heat to raise 40 C to 100 C plus the heat to vaporise the water}]
Water at temperature 40\textdegree C flows from a tap T into a heated container C. The container has a heating element (a resistor R) which is generating heat at the rate of P, that may be varied. The rate of water inflow from tap is m = $\dfrac{1000}{7}\ell$/min. The heated generated is sufficient so that the water in the container is boiling and getting converted into steam at a steady rate. The minimum power P (in MW) that must be generated as heat in the steady state in resistor R so that the amount of liquid water in the container neither increases nor decreases with time ? (Neglect other losses of heat, such as conduction from the container to the air and heat capacity of container)\par
For water, specific heat c = 4.2 kJ kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, latent heat of vaporization L$_\text{vap}$ = 2.268 MJ kg$^{-1}$, density $\rho$ = 1000 kg m$^{-3}$.\par
\bfig{117.6}{SA08_p2_phy_s3_q03_1.png}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SA23-P1-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score Advanced - Test 23 (14 Apr 2024)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=single, subtopic={Expansion}, answer={D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K3 S1 I2 C2 F0}, diff_note={concepts: apparent expansion of a liquid in a container, volume expansion of liquid, container | steps: volume expansion of liquid and container}]
At a certain temperature T, a liquid with volume $V_1$ and volumetric expansion coefficient $\alpha$ is at a certain level in a container. At the same temperature, a solid body with a volume $V_2$ and coefficient of linear expansion $\lambda$ remains outside the liquid. The temperature of the liquid in the container is reduced by $\Delta$T, and the temperature of the object is raised by an equal amount and then thrown into the container. In this case, the liquid level in the container does not change. How much $\Delta$T is required to achieve this situation? The densities and volumes of the object and the liquid are such that they allow the object to fully sink into the liquid. It will be assumed that the container does not expand, is heat insulating and that there will be no heat exchange between the liquid and the object.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$\dfrac{V_1-V_2}{\alpha V_1-3\lambda V_2}$}
\opt{B}{$\dfrac{V_1-V_2}{\alpha V_1-\lambda V_2}$}
\opt{C}{$\dfrac{V_1}{\alpha V_1-3\lambda V_2}$}
\opt{D}{$\dfrac{V_2}{\alpha V_1-3\lambda V_2}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA23-P1-PHY-S4-Q09, source={Score Advanced - Test 23 (14 Apr 2024)}, paper=1, qno=9, type=numerical, subtopic={Calorimetry}, answer={126}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K3 S1 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: final temperature of a lead copper water system, calorimetry, heat balance with specific heats | steps: heat balance with specific heats}]
A piece of lead of mass 0.600 kg and at a temperature of 373.0 K is placed in a copper vessel of mass 0.200 kg which contains of 0.500 kg of water at a temperature of 290.0 K. The final steady temperature of the mixture is 292.8 K. The specific heat capacity of copper is 386 J kg$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ and that the water is 4180 J kg$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$. Calculate the specific heat capacity of lead (in J kg K$^{-1}$). Assume that there is no work interactions and there is no heat exchange with the surrounding. [Give answer to nearest integer]
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA27-P2-PHY-S3-Q03, source={Score Advanced - Test 27 (24 Apr 2024)}, paper=2, qno=3, type=numerical, subtopic={Expansion}, answer={1}, answer_src=solved, working={Heating: Delta T = 1e-3/(8e-5 x 0.15) = 83.3 K, m = 9e3 x 4e-6 x 0.15 = 5.4e-3 kg, E1 = 5.4e-3 x 400 x 83.3 = 180 J. Stretching: E2 = 1/2 (135e9 x 4e-6/0.15)(1e-3)\^{}2 = 1.8 J. E1/E2 = 100, so x/100 = 1.}, difficulty=9, diff_parts={K3 S2 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: ratio of heat absorbed to elastic energy for the same elongation, expansion, DeltaT from the expansion | steps: DeltaT from the expansion; E1 = m c DeltaT; E2 = 1/2 (YA/L) x\^{}2}]
We would; like to increase the length of a 15 cm long copper rod of cross-section 4 mm$^2$ by 1 mm. The energy absorbed by the rod if it is heated is E$_1$. The energy stored by the rod if it is stretched slowly is E$_2$. Then find E$_1$ / E$_2$. If your answer is x fill value of x/100.\par
[Various parameters of Copper are : Density = 9 $\times$ 10$^3$ kg/m$^3$, Thermal coefficient of linear expansion = 8 $\times$ 10$^{-5}$ K$^{-1}$, Young's modulus = 135 $\times$ 10$^9$ Pa , Specific heat = 400 J / kg $-$ K]
\end{bankq}

\section*{Nurture SRG papers}
\begin{bankq}[id=NSRG03-P2-PHY-S1-Q01, source={Nurture SRG - Test 03 (04 Feb 2024)}, paper=2, qno=1, type=single, subtopic={Specific and latent heat}, answer={A}, answer_src=solved, working={$x(3.36)=(1-x)(21)$ per unit mass gives $86.2$ percent}, difficulty=3, diff_parts={K1 S1 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: freezing of water by evaporation under vacuum | steps: energy balance between freezing and evaporation; fraction frozen}]
A thermally insulated vessel contains some water at $0^\circ$C. The vessel is connected to a vacuum pump to pump out water vapour. This results in some water getting frozen. It is given Latent heat of vaporization of water at $0^\circ$C $=21\times10^5$ J/kg and latent heat of freezing of water $=3.36\times10^5$ J/kg. The maximum percentage amount of water that will be solidified in this manner will be :
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$86.2\%$}
\opt{B}{$33.6\%$}
\opt{C}{$21\%$}
\opt{D}{$24.36\%$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=NSRG03-P2-PHY-S2-Q07, source={Nurture SRG - Test 03 (04 Feb 2024)}, paper=2, qno=7, type=multi, subtopic={Specific and latent heat}, answer={A,D}, answer_src=solved, working={Steam produced at $4.44\times10^{-5}$ kg/s gives $7.67$ mm/s; heating the steam alone gives $\dfrac{nR}{PA}\cdot0.025=23.1$ mm/s}, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K1 S3 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: boiling and heating of steam under a piston | steps: rate of vaporisation; volume of steam; rate of rise at boiling; heating of steam; rate of rise after boiling}]
The bottom of the cylinder contains 2 kg of water at $100^\circ$C. The cylinder has a radius $\left(\dfrac{10}{\sqrt\pi}\right)$cm. The massless piston sits on the surface of water. An electric heater at the base of cylinder transfers energy into the water at the rate of 100 W. Assume the cylinder is of sufficient length so that piston never reaches the top of the cylinder. (Take $R=\dfrac{25}3$, $L_v=2.25\times10^6$J/kg and $S_{steam}=2000$ J/kg-$^\circ$C, $P_0=10^5\ \mathrm{N/m^2}$) Assume steam as an ideal gas.\par
\bfig{98.7}{NSRG03_p2_phy_s2_q07_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The rate of rise of piston when water starts boiling into steam is 7.67 mm/sec.}
\opt{B}{The rate of rise of piston when water starts boiling into steam is 1.2 mm/sec.}
\opt{C}{The rate of rise of piston when water has completely converted into steam is 12.6 mm/sec.}
\opt{D}{The rate of rise of piston when water has completely converted into steam is 23.1 mm/sec.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=TOAS11-P2-PHY-S3-Q05, source={TOAS - Test 11 (27 Jun 2022)}, paper=2, qno=5, type=numerical, subtopic={Calorimetry}, answer={12.00}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S2 I0 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: calorimetry with variable specific heat | steps: heat lost by the liquid by integration; heat lost by the calorimeter; heat gained by the ice through melting and warming; solve m}]
A calorimeter of water equivalent 10 gm contains a liquid of mass 50 gm at $40^\circ$C. When `$m$' gram of ice at $-10^\circ$C is put into the calorimeter and the mixture is allowed to attain equilibrium, the final temperature was found to be 20 $^\circ$C. It is known that specific heat capacity of the liquid changes with temperature as $S=\left(1+\dfrac{\theta}{500}\right)$ Cal g$^{-1}$ $^\circ$C$^{-1}$ where $\theta$ is temperature in $^\circ$C. The specific heat capacity of ice, water and colorimeter remains constant and values are $S_{\text{ice}}=0.5$ Cal g$^{-1}$ $^\circ$C$^{-1}$, $S_{\text{water}}=1.0$ Cal g$^{-1}$ $^\circ$C$^{-1}$ and latent heat of fusion of ice is $L_f=80$ Cal g$^{-1}$. Assume no heat loss to the surrounding and calculate the value of `$m$' in gram.
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=TOAS19-P1-PHY-S1-Q07, source={TOAS - Test 19 (05 Feb 2023)}, paper=1, qno=7, type=multi, subtopic={Calorimetry}, answer={B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=3, diff_parts={K1 S2 I0 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: mixing of ice and water | steps: heat available from water; mass melted; remaining ice; effect of the calorimeter}, also_in={TNAS - Test 01 (05 Feb 2023) P2 Q7}]

\opt{B}{The moment of inertia remains unchanged.}

\begin{bankq}[id=TOPS04-P2-PHY-S2-Q07, source={TOPS - Test 04 (18 Dec 2022)}, paper=2, qno=7, type=numerical, subtopic={Calorimetry}, answer={495.00}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: variable specific heat, calorimetry | steps: heat given by the container; heat taken by the ice; mass}]

\begin{bankq}[id=TOPS05-P1-PHY-S3-Q08, source={TOPS - Test 05 (14 Jan 2023)}, paper=1, qno=8, type=numerical, subtopic={Expansion}, answer={3.96}, answer_src=solved, working={Gap $=L\alpha\Delta T=12.0\times11\times10^{-6}\times30=3.96\times10^{-3}$ m $=3.96$ mm; the printed key shows 4.22, which would need $\alpha\approx11.7\times10^{-6}$}, difficulty=3, diff_parts={K1 S1 I0 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: thermal expansion | steps: expansion over the rise in temperature; gap}]
A railway track (made of iron) is laid in winter when the average temperature is 18$^\circ$C. The track consists of sections of 12.0 m placed one after the other. How much gap (in mm) should be left between two such sections so that there is no compression during summer when the maximum temperature goes to 48$^\circ$C ? Coefficient of linear expansion of iron $=11\times10^{-6}$ /$^\circ$C.
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=TOPS05-P2-PHY-S3-Q03, source={TOPS - Test 05 (14 Jan 2023)}, paper=2, qno=3, type=numerical, subtopic={Specific and latent heat}, answer={2}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K2 S3 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: variable specific heat, averages | steps: heat from 0 to t by integral; average heat capacity; heat capacity at t; difference; n}]
A 1kg substance of specific heat capacity is given as $C=(A+Bt^2)$, where $A$ and $B$ are constant and $t$ is temperature in $^\circ$C, is heated. Magnitude of difference in average heat capacity $\left(\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}\right)$ from $0^\circ$C to $t^\circ$C and heat capacity at $t^\circ$C is given as $\dfrac{4BT^2}{3n}$, find $n$.
\end{bankq}

\section*{TEAS papers}
\begin{bankq}[id=TEAS01-P1-PHY-S1-Q02, source={TEAS - Test 01 (16 Apr 2023)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=multi, subtopic={Calorimetry}, answer={A,B,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K2 S3 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: calorimetry, graph reading | steps: heat balance for cooling water; the temperature when melting starts; ice mass from the graph; final state; check each}]
A calorimeter was filled with 10 g of water at a temperature of 70$^\circ$C. To cool it down, the researchers threw in calorimeter some crushed ice from a freezer at temperature $-10\,^\circ$C. Latent heat of ice $=330$ kJ/kg, specific heat capacity of water and ice are $c_w=4200$ J/(kg $^\circ$C) and $c_i=2100$ J/(kg $^\circ$C) respectively Graphs of dependences of the mass of each of substances from time are given on the image. Unfortunately, scientists have spilled coffee on the graph, and part of the experimental data was lost. Help researchers recover these data by choosing the correct answers. Neglect any heat loss.
\bfig{153.3}{TEAS01_p1_phy_s1_q02_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The temperature of the water by the time the ice began to melt was 60$^\circ$C.}
\opt{B}{The final temperature in the calorimeter was 0$^\circ$C.}
\opt{C}{In steady state, 50\% was water and rest ice.}
\opt{D}{The mass of ice initially was 20 gm.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\section*{TMAS papers}
\begin{bankq}[id=TMAS03-P1-PHY-S1-Q01, source={TMAS - Test 03 (10 Sep 2023)}, paper=1, qno=1, type=multi, subtopic={Expansion}, answer={B,D}, answer_src=solved, working={Curvature of a bimetallic strip is $\propto|\alpha_B-\alpha_C|\Delta T$, so $R$ is inversely proportional to both}, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S1 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: bimetallic strip bending | steps: curvature from differential expansion; dependence on temperature and difference}]
A bimetallic strip is formed out of two identical strips, one of copper and other of brass. The coefficient of linear expansion of the two metals are $\alpha_c$ and $\alpha_B$ respectively. On heating, the temperature of the strip increases up by $\Delta T$ and the strip bends to form an arc of radius of curvature $R$. Then $R$ is :-
\bfig{108.2}{TMAS03_p1_phy_s1_q01_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Proportional to $\Delta T$.}
\opt{B}{Inversely proportional to $\Delta T$.}
\opt{C}{Proportional to $|\alpha_B-\alpha_C|$.}
\opt{D}{Inversely proportional to $|\alpha_B-\alpha_C|$.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=TNAS04-P1-PHY-S1-Q01, source={TNAS - Test 04 (18 Jun 2023)}, paper=1, qno=1, type=single, subtopic={Expansion}, answer={B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: thermal stress in a rod, spring in series | steps: thermal elongation; force balance with spring; solve for net elongation}]

Spring force on the rod acts uniformly over the cross section during elongation of the rod. Find the net elongation of the rod ? (Assume thermal strain to be small)
\bfig{161.3}{TNAS04_p1_phy_s1_q01_1.png}

\opt{A}{$\dfrac{k\ell_0\alpha\Delta\theta}{k+\frac{YA}{\ell_0}}$}

\opt{C}{$YA\alpha\Delta\theta$}
\opt{D}{None of these}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=TNAS04-P1-PHY-S3-Q02, source={TNAS - Test 04 (18 Jun 2023)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=single, subtopic={Expansion}, answer={60.52}, answer_src=solved, working={Floating condition $\rho_p/\rho_w=0.99$ with $\gamma_p=3\alpha=6.9\times10^{-5}$: $0.99(1+\gamma_w\Delta T)=1+\gamma_p\Delta T$ gives $\Delta T=\dfrac{0.01}{0.99\times3.19\times10^{-4}-6.9\times10^{-5}}=40.5^\circ$C, final temperature $60.5^\circ$C}, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: thermal expansion, floating bodies | steps: volume expansion of polymer; density condition for floating; solve for temperature rise; add initial temperature}]
A sphere made of polymer is floating on the surface of water which is at a temperature of $20^\circ$C and 1\% of the volume of the sphere is above the water. What final temperature (in $^\circ$C) must the water be heated in order to submerge the polymer sphere completely. Take coefficient of linear expansion of the polymer $2.30\times10^{-5}$ /$^\circ$C and coefficient of volume expansion of water is $3.19\times10^{-4}$ /$^\circ$C.
\end{bankq}
